primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'great fish' (Jonah's fish, sometimes rendered 'sea-monster'/ketos) is read primarily as a type or foreshadowing of Christ's death, burial, and resurrection: the three days and nights Jonah spent in the fish's belly prefigure Jesus' three days in the grave ('the sign of Jonah'). The fish's belly is correspondingly understood as an image of the grave/Sheol/death, from which God delivers. The fish itself is generally treated not as an agent of evil but as an instrument of God's judgment-and-deliverance (divine providence).
primary_basis: Jonah 2:1-10 (esp. 2:2, 'out of the belly of Sheol')
Matthew 12:39-41 ('the sign of the prophet Jonah')
1 Corinthians 15:4 (raised 'on the third day according to the Scriptures,' often linked to Jonah typology)

alternatives.meaning: The fish/sea-monster (tannin, Leviathan, Rahab) as a symbol of chaos, evil, hostile cosmic powers, or Satan, subdued by God; also applied to hostile nations (Egypt's Pharaoh, Babylon) portrayed as sea-monsters.
Fish more broadly as a symbol of Christ (the early Christian ICHTHYS acrostic) and of believers gathered by the gospel ('fishers of men'; the net full of fish as the church/kingdom).
basis: Early church usage (e.g., Tertullian, On Baptism 1; catacomb iconography)

alternatives.meaning: Jonah's fish as emphasizing divine providence, rescue, and preservation (a vehicle of salvation and second chances) rather than a symbol of the tomb per se; common in devotional and homiletical treatment.
basis: Jonah 1:17 ('the LORD appointed a great fish')

alternatives.meaning: A literal-historical, non-symbolic reading: the great fish is simply a real creature God used; any 'meaning' is limited to the sign Jesus assigns it, with no independent symbolism.
Allegorical-critical reading in which the fish represents Babylon and the exile: Jonah stands for Israel swallowed by Babylon and later 'vomited out' (return from exile).
basis: Jonah read as post-exilic parable in some critical scholarship

alternatives.meaning: Patristic/medieval spiritualizing readings in which the sea-monster represents death, hell, or the devil, whom Christ enters and defeats from within (the 'baited hook' motif of atonement).
basis: Homiletic use of Job 41 and Jonah 2 in patristic literature

notes: The parenthetical 'great fish, sea-monster' points chiefly to Jonah 1:17 (LXX ketos, echoed in Matthew 12:40). Christian interpretation of that specific image is unusually settled because Jesus himself supplies the interpretation ('the sign of Jonah'), making the death-burial-resurrection typology the dominant reading across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions from the church fathers onward. Distinctions matter, however: 'fish' in general (ichthys, fishers of men) carries a separate, positive Christ/church symbolism, while 'sea-monster/dragon' (tannin, Leviathan) in the Old Testament carries a largely negative chaos/evil symbolism; conflating these three strands would misstate the consensus. The Hebrew text of Jonah says 'great fish' (dag gadol), not a monster, and mainstream interpreters generally do not identify Jonah's fish with the hostile Leviathan-type creatures.
